### What a predictable day does for the brain (executive function)

The Center on the Developing Child at Harvard describes a set of mental skills that let a child hold a plan in mind, resist a pull in another direction and shift when something changes (executive function). Its 2011 working paper names three parts. Holding information in mind while using it (working memory). Stopping an impulse long enough to choose (inhibitory control). Switching to a new rule or a new way (cognitive flexibility). They grow fastest between about three and five, through practice in settings steady enough that a child can predict what comes next and take part in it.

When a child knows that snack follows small group and that the chicken bucket goes out after snack, the mind is free for the work in front of it, and the routine itself gives the practice. The Center's 2014 guide of practices by age shows how that practice changes.

- **Twos and threes.** A short, repeated sequence with the same words each time, one step at a time, songs with movements that stop and start, and a steady adult close by to borrow from (co-regulation). The Idea bank card The same song for moving carries this.
- **Threes and fours.** Two or three steps held at once, a picture schedule children helped make, simple games with a rule that changes, and jobs with a known order, such as scraping, rinsing and telling an educator they are done. The Idea bank card Time in our day holds the picture schedule.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** Planning out loud before starting, carrying a multi step job such as setting a table from the roster, checking their own work against a picture guide, and showing a younger child the sequence.

The research found that these skills predict later learning and health, and that practice strengthens them. It did not find that any one routine does this on its own, so we hold the whole day as the practice.

### Care routines as curriculum (Magda Gerber)

Magda Gerber, who founded Resources for Infant Educarers in 1978 after working with the pediatrician Emmi Pikler in Budapest, taught that the moments adults often hurry through, diapering, dressing, feeding and washing hands, are the heart of the curriculum for the youngest children. The adult slows down, tells the child what is about to happen, waits for the child's response, and involves the child in the task with their own hands. A child who hears "I am going to lift you now" and has a moment to ready their body is a participant in their own care.

Gerber's claim rests on her observation and on Pikler's long records at the Lóczy institute, with no controlled trials behind it, and that is how we hold it. In West class, handwashing, shoes going on before leaving the rest area and the walk to the piazza belong to the curriculum. Each is a place where a child practices doing for themselves, with an adult who narrates and waits. The Idea bank card A block of clay at arrival shows the same idea at the start of the day, one material that lets hands settle while the goodbye happens.

### What transitions ask of children

Virginia Vitiello and colleagues followed children across whole preschool days in 2012 and found that children's positive engagement was lower during transitions than during free choice and small group. Mary Louise Hemmeter and colleagues, writing in 2008 from the Pyramid Model work, describe transitions as the time of day when challenging behavior is most likely, and list what lowers it. Fewer transitions, shorter ones, a warning ahead, a clear picture of what comes next, and something to do during the wait.

That is the research behind our 30 minute allowance for a full move, the finger count warnings, the list and the face check at every gate, and the job handed to a child who finds moving hard. A child carrying the bucket has a plan to hold in mind (working memory) and a reason to keep walking. The Idea bank cards Helping in the animal yards and The same song for moving hold the set-ups.

### The core roles

- **Why it matters.** The roles are named in Educator Duties and Procedures, Policies and Procedures. The line on following the schedule is from the PD Days deck, August 10, 2026.

### What the group gives a child (Malaguzzi and Paley)

Loris Malaguzzi, founder of the Reggio Emilia schools, held that a child is a social being from birth and that relationships and learning happen in the same moment. In the interview published in The Hundred Languages of Children in 1993 he described the small group of two to five children as the most favorable size for learning, because in it a child meets other minds close enough to argue with, borrow from and build on. Knowledge is built between people (co-construction), and the educator's work is to listen for it. Carlina Rinaldi later named that stance a pedagogy of listening. Our morning small groups follow this directly, and meeting time is where the small groups bring what they found back to the whole class.

Vivian Gussin Paley, a kindergarten educator at the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools for most of her career, wrote more than a dozen books from her own transcripts of children talking. Wally's Stories (1981) and The Boy Who Would Be a Helicopter (1990) show what a group conversation does when the adult writes down children's exact words and reads them back. Her practice of story dictation and story acting, in which a child tells a story, the educator writes it and the class acts it out the same day, gave every child a reason to listen to every other child. Ageliki Nicolopoulou and colleagues tested that practice in Head Start classes in 2015 and found gains in children's narrative skill, print awareness and their ability to wait and take turns (self-regulation), which is more than Paley claimed for it herself. In You Can't Say You Can't Play (1992) she used meeting time for a yearlong conversation with five year olds about one rule, and let the children decide it. Our Question of the day on chart paper, read back at the next meeting, is Paley's method at our size. The Idea bank card Chart paper, living documentation holds the set-ups.

### How attention and self-regulation grow

How long a child can attend to a group, and what helps, changes across our three classes. The claim often repeated that children attend for a few minutes per year of age has no study behind it, so we watch bodies instead. Elena Bodrova and Deborah Leong, building on Lev Vygotsky in Tools of the Mind (2007), describe self-regulation as growing from the outside in. A child first regulates others, telling a friend to wait, then uses outside helps such as a song, a prop or a picture, then talks themselves through it (private speech), and at last holds the rule inside. The listening ear card and the talking mouth card they used for turn-taking are the kind of outside help a child can hold. Adele Diamond and colleagues found in 2007 that the program improved children's cognitive control, and later larger trials found mixed results, so what we keep is the mechanism, which Vygotsky's own work supports. Claims about any one program stay open.

- **Twos and threes.** A short gathering, a song with movements, one book or one object, and freedom to come and go with an adult nearby. A child regulates mostly by borrowing from a steady adult (co-regulation). A chair can give a body what it needs.
- **Threes and fours.** A Question of the day with each child's answer beside their name, a puppet to try the words of asking for a turn, a movement break between topics, and a child beginning to wait while a friend speaks because the chart shows their turn is coming.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** Looking back at yesterday's photos and planning today, class agreements written in children's own words, a story acted out, a problem about turns brought to the group and decided there, and children who echo one another before the educator does.

The Idea bank cards Meeting time, Looking back at today and Taking turns in a community of care hold the set-ups for each band, and Music and movement holds the songs and the movement breaks.

### Preparing together

### The child between two worlds (Bronfenbrenner)

Urie Bronfenbrenner, in The Ecology of Human Development (1979), described a child growing inside a set of nested settings. The closest are the places the child lives in directly, home, our school, a grandparent's house (the microsystem). The connections between those places (the mesosystem) are a setting of their own, and Bronfenbrenner argued that a child does better when the adults in two microsystems know each other, share information and hold each other in regard. Further out are settings the child never enters that still shape their day, such as a parent's workplace or licensing rules (the exosystem), and the wider culture and its values (the macrosystem). He later added time, the changes in a family and a society across years (the chronosystem).

The theory is a frame for seeing, and it has not been tested as one piece. What the research since has found is narrower and steady. When families and programs communicate often and in both directions (reciprocal communication), children settle into school more easily and their early learning is stronger. For us the mesosystem is the home visit, the daily check-in at the door, the Family page in TREE and the Proud Moment that shows a family how their child thinks. Each one strengthens the link between the two places a child lives.

### Six kinds of partnership (Epstein) and what families know (Moll and González)

Joyce Epstein at Johns Hopkins University, in 1995, named six kinds of involvement a school can build, and the framework still shapes how family engagement is studied. Parenting, helping families with the home conditions that support a child. Communicating, in both directions. Volunteering, in ways that fit a family's hours and strengths. Learning at home, with ideas families can use. Decision making, with families on committees and in planning. Collaborating with the community, connecting families to resources. Epstein's surveys found that schools vary widely in which of the six they practice, and that families' involvement follows what the school invites. Our family participation hours, the Parent Advisory Council (PAC), the learning at home invitations and the family evenings cover all six, and the list is a useful check on which one a class has let go quiet.

Luis Moll, Norma González, Cathy Amanti and Deborah Neff, working in Tucson in 1992, sent educators into students' homes as learners. They found that every household held bodies of skill and knowledge built up over generations so the family could get by, in building, farming, cooking, healing, trade, music and language, and they named these funds of knowledge. When educators drew on them, children's families became sources of curriculum. The study was small and qualitative, in Mexican American households, and it is best read as a stance. Our home visit, the All About Me book, the family recipes cooked in the culinary atelier, and the invitation for a family to share a skill, a song or a trade at meeting time are that stance in practice. The Idea bank cards Family and babies and Cooking and food hold the set-ups, and Seeing Ourselves describes the family wall and the books.

### Participation as a value (Rinaldi and Cadwell)

In Reggio Emilia, families were in the schools from the beginning, since families built the first ones after the war. Carlina Rinaldi, in In Dialogue with Reggio Emilia, writes about participation as one of the values the schools were founded on, with families, educators and children as co-authors of a school that is always being made, and about documentation as what makes that participation possible, because a family can respond to what they can see. Louise Boyd Cadwell, in Bringing Reggio Emilia Home (1997) and Bringing Learning to Life (2003), describes the St. Louis schools learning to do this in an American setting, with families reading documentation on the walls, joining projects and asking the questions that moved them. Both writers describe practice, and neither claims a measured outcome. What they give us is the reason our family evenings run as provocations, why the weekly newsletter carries children's words, and why a conference opens with documentation and the Family Summary.

### Welcoming a new family

What they give us is the reason our family evenings run as provocations, why the weekly newsletter carries children's words, and why a conference opens with documentation and the Family Summary.

changes.from: ### A team that shares the work
changes.to:
### Who decides what (Ellyn Satter)

Ellyn Satter, a dietitian and family therapist, set out in Child of Mine (1983) a division of responsibility in feeding that pediatric and dietetic bodies have cited ever since. The adult decides what food is offered, when and where. The child decides whether to eat and how much. Each side keeps to its own job. The adult offers a varied table at steady times, sits down to eat with the child, and does not coax, praise, bargain or restrict. The child comes to the table, may say no, may eat a lot one day and little the next, and over time learns to trust their own fullness (self-regulation of intake). Satter's model rests on clinical work and on the feeding research of others more than on trials of the model itself, which is worth knowing. What the trials of its parts found is below.

Our Meal Time Values are Satter's division almost word for word. We provide the setting, the food and the tools. Each child chooses what and how much.

### What Leann Birch found

Leann Birch, a developmental psychologist at Penn State, ran the experiments that stand behind most of what programs say about children and food.

- **Repeated exposure.** With Diane Marlin in 1982, Birch offered two year olds unfamiliar foods between five and twenty times and found that preference rose with the number of tastes, with eight to ten before many children accepted a food. A 1987 study with Birch found that looking at a food did not do it. Tasting did.
- **Wariness of new foods (food neophobia).** Reluctance to taste anything unfamiliar rises around age two, is strongest from about two to six, and eases through childhood. Terence Dovey and colleagues reviewed this in 2008 and found it ordinary and partly inherited, and found that the same exposure effect works on it.
- **Rewards and pressure.** Birch, Marlin and Rotter in 1984 found that rewarding a child for eating a food lowered the child's liking for it afterward. Jennifer Fisher and Birch in 1999 found that restricting a food raised children's eating of it once it was available. Pressure in either direction works against the child's own learning.
- **Watching others.** Birch found in 1980 that preschoolers seated with friends who chose a different vegetable shifted their own choice within days, and the shift held weeks later. Adults eating the same food at the table has shown the same effect in later studies.

Birch gathered this work in her 1999 review. The studies were small, in American preschools, and eight to ten is an average, so a child who needs fifteen is within the range. Family-style serving gives all four findings a daily place. Research comparing family-style with pre-plated meals for how much children eat is mixed, so what we claim is the skills and the social meal.

### How the table grows (and Malaguzzi on the kitchen)

In the Reggio Emilia schools the kitchen is open and in view, the cook is a member of the educational team who joins staff meetings, and children go in and out. The buildings were planned under Malaguzzi with the kitchen and the piazza at the center so that eating would be a shared, visible part of the day and the cook a known adult. Our Kitchen window, the chef's notes on the menu and the Unicorn Café follow that plan. The Idea bank cards Piazza and culinary atelier and Cooking and food hold the knife grips, the tool agreements and the recipes.

- **Twos and threes.** Tongs and a small pitcher, one scoop to start, tasting and spitting out allowed, an educator who names each food and eats it, and a serrated tomato knife on soft fruit with an adult beside each child.
- **Threes and fours.** Spreading their own toppings, pouring for a friend, the bridge and claw grips, saying "I'm done" in words, and following the piazza picture guide on their own.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** Setting a table from the roster, serving courses, the mini santoku, writing café menus, harvesting one garden food from bed to bowl and showing a younger child the sequence.

### A team that shares the work

- [Development of Food Preferences, Leann L. Birch, Annual Review of Nutrition, 1999](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.nutr.19.1.41)
- [Food Neophobia and Picky or Fussy Eating in Children, A Review, Terence M. Dovey, Paul A. Staples, E. Leigh Gibson and Jason C. G. Halford, Appetite, 2008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appet.2007.09.009)
